5.105.m: The sages said: / "After this, what did that fortunate Rāghava do? / And what did the great-souled sages do after that?"
Sūta said: "When Rāmacandra, Vibhīṣaṇa, and the lord of monkeys were seated comfortably, / the excellent sages said to Śambhu, 'Tell us an auspicious story.'"
Hearing their words, Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī: / "This exceedingly lovely house belongs to a certain brāhmaṇa,
adorned with delightful groves, ponds, and creepers, / where the god whose weapon is flowers is summoned by the hum of swarms of bees.
The sun sets about mounting the noon junction, as it were; / having bathed in the cool waters of the pond, wearing fine garments,
anointed with excellent sandalwood and camphor rubbed with musk, / with firmly tied braids adorned with garlands of sallakī flowers,
chewing in turns betel with abundant camphor, / tasting it, intoxicated, both rejoicing, where in a lovely shower-house,
rich with the calls of peacocks, with sweet songs outside, / and reclining together comfortably on a bed that is spread out,
if that face with broad smile and red lips is kissed, / then the fruit of worldly existence will be savoured by the two of us."
Hearing what was spoken thus, those sages became enraged: / "Is this very auspicious speech that was uttered by you to us?
Rambling born of attachment to your beloved was uttered; our word was not heeded!" / Then, from the mouth of Śambhu, who was given over to wrath, an exceedingly wondrous
flame emerged, and it assumed a terrifying face; / then it swiftly approached the wife of a certain sage.
She was intent on fleeing, and seeing Rāma, she became frightened; / Rāma too said, "I shall release the pure brāhmaṇa woman!"
He departed by the Puṣpaka alone, speaking repeatedly of release, / and Rāghava did not remember to fix an arrow to his bow.
Śambhu too, having seen exceedingly sacred forests, sanctuaries, / and wondrous cities, did not remember Rāma.
And in an instant the great mountain Lokāloka was reached; / then Rāghava, having seen the mountain crowded with paths to dwellings, [asked:]
"Where has the fortunate brāhmaṇa woman gone? Tell me, O twice-born ones!" / They said to him, "She has gone this way, into the dark region of the mountain."
Rāma, his face pale, thought, "Alas, what distress!" / Then Śambhu of great splendor bestowed unequalled radiance.
By the power of that light, Rāma followed the sorceress. / It was a vast region composed of darkness, devoid of any living creatures,
extending to the edge of the cosmic egg, a hundred crore yojanas in measure. / And in the midst of that darkness stood a great silver land.
There was the city of Nārāyaṇa, radiant as ten million suns. / Seeing it, Rāma and the best of sages were struck with wonder.
Thinking, "What is this? How could our entrance be possible? / Could this be the fire of cosmic dissolution created by the Supreme Self's māyā?
Or will our death happen today, or will it bring good fortune?" / While the sages along with Rāma were thus filled with anxiety,
Śambhu said: "Listen now, Rāghava, I tell this to you: / I created this wondrous illusion for your sake.
This is the supreme, radiant abode belonging to Nārāyaṇa, / unaffected by heat, cold, and the like, accessible to knowledge and invisible to the physical eye.
Look up above at those worshiping it, led by Brahmā; / and look at the immaculate sages worshiping it in all the directions.
Behold the four Vedas praising the supreme abode. / The yogins led by Sanaka, diligently practicing yoga,
meditate upon this supreme splendor—behold it, Rāghava! / Look at this Romaśa performing circumambulations and prostrations,
and the lordly sages, the Vālakhilyas, in their tens of millions. / Behold the supreme abode worshiped by Lakṣmī and all the goddesses,
proclaimed as Brahman both with form and without form. / The ignorant do not see it; those with the eye of knowledge see it."
Therefore, at Śambhu's word, they all worshiped Acyuta / with girikarṇī flowers, tulasī, jasmine, and māruta,
with blue lotuses, water lilies, and dark blossoming waters. / The great-souled ones worshiped the great-souled Janārdana.
Then in the sky they beheld Nārada, matted-haired, with his vīṇā, / proclaiming the name of Nārāyaṇa, wearing a sacred thread, with a long beard.
Nārada too wondered in his mind: "Who is this?" / Filled with bliss, he fell at the feet of the Lord, Śambhu.
In his mind the sage chanted the Śaiva five-syllable mantra: / "Blessed am I, graced am I; my birth has become fruitful today!
I have known your state, revered by Brahmā and the gods, yet inaccessible!" / Then Śambhu said to Nārada: "Do not speak thus!
Conduct yourself in such a way that they do not know me. / Go quickly and tell Hari of my quiet arrival."
Then, going swiftly, he announced everything to Hari. / Thereupon Viṣṇu, swiftly taking auspicious arghya water,
accompanied by Kamalā, a yogin surrounded by tens of millions [of attendants], / the one whose banner is Garuḍa went out, holding Nārada by the hand.
Saying, "Homage, homage, homage be to this Śaṅkara!", / Keśava worshiped all of them with arghya, water for washing feet, and other offerings.
The boundless-spirited one ushered them into the auspicious city of Nārāyaṇa. / Standing then in the king of palaces, Nārāyaṇa said:
"How have these arrived? Who is this glorious king? / This is an entrance unachievable by mortals, beyond the reach even of Brahmā and the gods."
Śambhu said: "Just as we arrived in the garb of sages, so did this king. / And this valiant King Rāmacandra is an amśa of yours.
He desires to see this wife of yours, Keśava." / Nārāyaṇa said, "So be it," and told Rāghava, "Enter!"
Then, entering the chamber, seeing Lakṣmī, bowing to her, / and humbling himself with modesty, he spoke words of noble conduct:
"I have achieved my purpose, there is no doubt. But tell me, what do you think?" / The blessed Goddess said: "You are young, handsome, and drawn by love, Rāghava.
That Sītā of lovely limbs was your wife; / separated from her, you were formerly deeply tormented by longing.
Tell me all of that, or else you will not leave!" / Hearing those playful words that ravish the minds of young men,
the self-restrained Rāmabhadra, having heard all of them, / desired to depart from there, bowing down to her lotus face.
Tormenting the crest-jewel of the Raghus with the lotus-arrow of Kama, / the goddess Padmā, lover of lotus groves, followed right behind him as he went out.
Knowing his vow of having only one wife, they approached Rāma. / Then, seeing the king whose limbs were trembling and whose feet stumbled as he walked,
Śiva and Nārāyaṇa were filled with supreme wonder: / "Ah, the firmness in the heart of him whose self was not overcome even by the goddess of illusion!
I see his steadfast courage here; surely because of that Rāma is renowned. / Everywhere around him there is only auspiciousness; nowhere is there inauspiciousness for him."
Then Rāma spoke these words: "Lord, O venerable one, I shall depart." / Then, permitted by Hari, that Rāghava, aboard the Puṣpaka,
departed together with the sage, together with Śambhu, and together with Nārāyaṇa. / He quickly went to Lokāloka, and from there to the Sweet-Water Ocean.
From there he traversed the continents and oceans, and returned to Jambūdvīpa. / He stood at the hermitage of Bharadvāja on the bank of the Gautamī.
Then, having bathed in the great river, the glorious Bharadvāja, lord of sages, / surrounded by his disciples, beheld the Puṣpaka [chariot].
Having duly honored the mighty-armed Rāma, Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, and the sages there, / the great sage said to them:
"You ought to take a meal in my hermitage, best of men." / Rāma, at the word of the sage, somehow said, "So be it."
Then, after bathing in the great river and offering libations to the gods and others, / when Rāma wished to eat, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words:
"Dharma would be abandoned, Rāma, if the śrāddha is not performed." / The blessed Rāma said: "On the new moon, during an eclipse, at a sacred ford, at Vyatīpāta, and at a solstice,
if an omitted śrāddha is to be performed again, O venerable one, / yet your instruction was that one should not perform a daily śrāddha again.
Just as in my case, when the death of my mothers occurred, / and ritual impurity had set in, the daily śrāddha was indeed not performed;
yet at the times of Vyatīpāta and the like it was performed according to your word." / Vasiṣṭha said: "All these sages are here, as well as this brāhmaṇa, Śambhu;
from his mouth the decision will be made in full." / All the sages, having resolved together, said to Śambhu:
"Tell us in full, O best of brāhmaṇas, you are great." / Śambhu said: "Which śrāddha must be omitted and which must indeed be performed again
when ritual impurity arises or during hindrances, I shall explain. / All monthly śrāddhas and water-pot offerings,
and the annual śrāddha, they know to be due after the ritual impurity ends. / As many other rites as were omitted during ritual impurity when a hindrance arose,
all of them must certainly be performed afterward; of this there is no doubt. / All monthly śrāddhas and likewise the annual śrāddha
must be performed after ritual impurity ends, or when any other hindrance occurs, as otherwise prescribed. / On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, one who desires good fortune should perform it.
If there is a transgression in that matter, it is performed on the new moon day. / Just so, it must be performed on the subsequent days if there is no hindrance.
In the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, it should be performed, Rāma, if not already done. / When the month of the day of death is not known in any way,
the śrāddha is prescribed on that day in Mārgaśīrṣa or in Māgha. / When the day is unknown but the month is known,
the annual śrāddha should be performed on the new moon day of that month. / When neither the day nor the month is known for one who died abroad,"
That lunar day is to be taken as that day when knowledge of it arises. / The new moon of Āśvina, the new moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, and the new moon of Māgha—these three days:
Any one of these is to be taken when the day and month are not known. / The ancestral rites for prosperity, seventh-month hair-parting, rites for the deceased spirit, monthly rites,
And the daily water-jar ancestral rite, are performed even in an intercalary month; / Also during an eclipse, on the birth of a son and the like, in pacification rites,
And in all rites previously resolved upon, an intercalary month is not defective. / When a man falls ill as the time for an ancestral rite approaches,
He should appoint his wife, his brother, or his disciple. / In his absence, the rite called śrāddha would suffer loss.
In the daily ancestral rite, one should appoint an eater according to one's means; / But in the new moon and monthly rite, and whatever is not the death anniversary,
If one is personally incapable of the rite, one should appoint a son or a brāhmaṇa. / For one engaged in royal business, or one caught in captivity as a servant,
And in all distresses, one should have the ancestral rite performed through a brāhmaṇa. / The best of the twice-born do not perform an ancestral rite in the morning;
In occasional ancestral rites, no strict rule of time is prescribed.
Except for household matters and the like, the kutupa period is remembered as the commencement; / Or it may be just prior to kutupa, closely bordering upon kutupa.
Just as in the monthly ancestral rite touching the afternoon is prescribed, / When the new moon spans the afternoon on both [consecutive] days,
In case of waning the earlier one is to be observed, but in waxing or equality the later is prescribed. / But when the new moon is equal across both afternoons,
In waning the earlier, in waxing the later, and in equality it should also be the later. / Where the moon has waned, there the pārvaṇa ancestral rite is held.
If on the eighth part of the new moon it is subtle, and on the eighth part of the fourteenth it is absent, / Then the lunar day spanning midday should be used for the single-ancestor rite.
The lunar day that spans the evening is the one for the pārvaṇa rite. / A new moon extending slightly into the afternoon is to be taken for ancestral rites and the like.
On the death anniversary, a lunar day lasting three muhūrtas in the evening time [is taken]; / When on the next day it has set, lasting three muhūrtas as before,
An ancestral rite on that next day would cause the destruction of the eldest son. / As one would perform the new-moon ancestral rite when the death anniversary arrives,
The lunar day spanning midday is prescribed there for the twice-born. / Rāma said: The entire sequence of the ancestral rite, as well as the sequence of mortal rites,
And the determination of incidental duties, you ought to declare. / Śambhu said: When the day of the ancestral rite arrives, having observed restraints on the preceding day,
He should invite eminent brāhmaṇas endowed with the marks of a brāhmaṇa. / Eating once a day, celibacy, not speaking with outcasts and the like,
Cleaning teeth, anointing with oil, and cutting nails and hair: / The performer should do these on the preceding day, and having abandoned them on the next day,
He should undertake the spoken vows and renounce all this. / If there is worship at the three junctures, he should worship his deity in the morning.
If he performs worship at the time of dawn, / Having slept on the ground in that manner, rising in the morning, knowing the rites,
Having performed whatever is the morning rite preceded by bathing, / Freed from the three debts, he will attain the supreme Brahman.
He who performs the worship of Śiva at the time of sunrise, / Splendid as the sun, is exalted in the realm of Śiva.
After the sun has risen, worship performed within the next ghaṭikā: / Splendid as Rudra, he is exalted in the realm of Śiva.
If he performs the worship of Śiva in the third ghaṭikā: / Splendid as Kubera, he is exalted in the realm of Śiva.
If he performs the worship of Śiva in the third ghaṭikā: / Splendid as Kubera, he is exalted in the realm of Śiva.
He who during the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh ghaṭikās / Worships Śiva with devotion, becomes like the Maruts in the realm of Śiva.
The worship is performed at that very time, at whatever time it has been declared; / Or, having undertaken the vow, he should worship according to his solemn promise.
He should maintain the vow in the services according to his ability; / Or, if there should be a transgression of the vow, yet the sacrifice belongs to the omnipresent Lord.
The illustrious Rāma said: Where is the worship of the God of gods, of Śaṅkara of boundless splendor, / Who destroys sins through remembrance and grants liberation through remembrance,
Of Śiva, of auspicious form, who knows the reality of Śiva's truth, / With the moon, adorned with the moon, moon-eyed, radiant,
The embodiment of the Veda and the formless, the essence of the Veda, the knower, / The knower of the Veda and Vedāṅgas, the yogin known and unknown,
Whose body is like cow's milk, who delights in bathing in cow's milk, / The protector of cows, three-eyed, having the three Vedas as eyes, the master of māyā?
In the midst of the inquiry, Śiva-knowledge was imparted to Rāma; / Sitting like an immovable pillar, fixing his eyes on the tip of his nose,
With the region of his cheeks touched by streams of tears of flowing bliss, / He held the god Giriśa, whose body was very smooth and handsome like cow's milk, in the lotus of his heart.
Then a reflection was seen upon Rāma's body; / Seeing Śambhu reflected, four-armed and three-eyed,
All the sages and lords of monkeys attained the highest amazement. / Seeing Rāma of radiant and auspicious form resting on Śambhu's chest,
They remained silent for half a watch, and then Rāma looked up. / Keeping his question in mind, he said: “Speak everything.”
Śambhu said: Whether in an immovable [object] worship is perpetual, or in a movable one as desired, / Worship of the liṅga is foremost; when it is not obtained, [it is done] in images and the like.
Worship is performed in each case according to specific qualification. / Worship of the liṅga is fruitful, whether devoid of qualities or endowed with qualities.
Worship performed in images and the like without qualities is indeed not fruitful; / Worship in a liṅga, whether immovable or movable, is praised.
I shall declare the worship of the movable [liṅga], as well as installation and dismissal; / Even a sage rarely knows both of those anywhere.
Yogins constantly install the Lord of gods, Śaṅkara, in the lotus of the heart, / Conceal him, worship him, and dismiss him.
For hotṛ-priests, the rite is in the fire for the three-eyed god; / For all worshippers, Maheśvara is in the Śiva-liṅga.
Installation of the liṅga, worship, dismissal, / And wearing Śaṅkara as the very liṅga, Maheśvara:
A casket of the highest excellence should be fashioned of gold, / Or made with silver plates, or made of silver and bamboo,
Or fashioned with cords of creepers, or of wood, / Or fashioned of cloth, or it may be crafted from clay.
Wrapped there in cloth endowed with fragrant perfume, / In a pure pair of washed cloths, provided with a soft seat,
Free from cold and heat, furnished with four legs, / Provided with a covering and lining, free from worms and insects,
One should envelop that Śiva on all sides with clean, soft cloth; / Placing the all-pervading Lord in the middle of the casket and covering him again:
This casket, O Rāma, is called the one before the god. / And his installation, recitation, and secret [worship] of the Great Lord,
Or it may be at the base of a wall, or on an altar for the deity; / In a well-protected place, one should also post a guard.
One should make it inseparable from one's life-breaths and the like, along with observances; / This indeed is declared to be the rājasika installation of the Supreme Self.
The sāttvika [mode] is keeping it near oneself, but the tāmasika is wearing it; / Wearing it involves touching the body and concealing the entire body.
Wearing it upon the head is foremost, and was done thus by Brahmā; / having placed it inside a crown, wearing it is said to be auspicious.
Wearing it on the forehead is commended, just as it was auspiciously borne by Lakṣmī; / and it was worn on the head by Bāṇa, or again upon the right side of his chest.
And on the ear by the supreme sage, the ascetic Harakarṇa, / and having pierced his body and fashioned an iron holder,
certain noble rākṣasas likewise wear the liṅga. / For homeless mortals who are infirm, bearing it upon the head is prescribed.
Wearing it at the waist knot and the like is declared to be the lowest of the low; / but among those, if food scraps touch it, it must be worn upon the head.
The constant wearing of the liṅga by those of the lowest of low conduct / is a wonder even for sinners; there is none in the realm of Yama.
Śrī Rāma said: / That firm writing which is inscribed upon the forehead by Citragupta, / hell is surely decreed by that writing; how is it otherwise?
He performs the worship of Śambhu; how does it destroy sin? / Śambhu said: / It destroys all sin, even that accumulated over hundreds of births,
from the scolding away of all sins and from remembering the Great Lord. / 'Ash' is declared to be the word for it; wearing it is supreme.
Indeed, by applying the semen of fire according to rule upon the forehead, / one would destroy the inscription of Yama like fire consumes that on a cloth.
A sin committed above the ear is destroyed when it is worn on the face, / and from wearing it upon the neck, sin committed by speech and the like is destroyed.
Sin committed by the arms [is destroyed] on the arms; that committed by the mind, on the chest; / sin committed with the penis, on the navel; and likewise that committed with the anus, on the back.
From wearing it upon the two flanks, O Rāma, that which arises from embracing another's wife [is destroyed]; / therefore the wearing of ash is commended everywhere as the three horizontal lines.
It is the bearing of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, and of the three sacred fires; / and it was worn by him for the protection of the three worlds.
Pure ash consecrated with mantras is worn in fifteen places: / on the two sides of the belly, on the two arms, and likewise on the pair above the belly,
wearing it on all bodies is agreed by dharma to be for worship. / Those who eat ash, sleep on ash, and have their bodies smeared with ash,
and bathe in ash are always freed from sins; there is no doubt in this. / Formerly, at the initiation of a brāhmaṇa, the [verse] 'Triyāyuṣa' is remembered.
It is a protector at the childbirth of mortals, and even against possession by spirits; / and for the sake of counteracting the poison of snakes and the like, this is the means for all.
Whether a mortal is a Vaiṣṇava, or even another person, / one who bathes in ash and is endowed with ash is qualified for religious rites.
Śrī Rāma said: / Tell me first the glorification of ash; for whom does ash grant long life? / And how indeed does this protect? Tell me all of this.
Śambhu said: / It is the cause for increasing the lifespan even of the threefold embodied being; / it is sin-destroying, cool and hot, and by touch it bestows the state of Śiva.
In this regard, I shall tell you an ancient legendary history. / There was a twice-born named Dhanañjaya, born in the lineage of Vasiṣṭha.
He had a hundred wives, endowed with beauty and charm. / Among them, one wife, Śāmākā, gave birth to Karuṇa, O sage.
There were as many ascetic sons as there were wives, O Rāma; / and an unequal partition of property was arranged for them by the father.
And then indeed a great bond of enmity arose among the brothers; / indeed, enmity among men of the same class is certain.
Then that Karuṇa went to the bank of the Bhavanāśinī, / together with various throngs of sages, desiring to see Narasiṃha.
For the purpose of seeing Nṛsiṃha, a certain brāhmaṇa / brought an eminent fruit, beautiful and fragrant.
Karuṇa, taking that supreme fruit, smelled it; / the groups of twice-born staying there afflicted him with a curse:
'Become a fly, O evil-minded one, for a hundred years from now; / the end of the curse will be brought about by the noble Dadhīca.'
Then, having been turned into a fly, he said this to his wife: / 'I have been turned into a fly; O auspicious one, protect me!'

Having spoken thus, having become so, he wandered here and there;
then, recognizing him to be in such a state, his kin, whose intentions were wicked,
making an effort to kill him, dropped him into oil. / Then, taking her dead husband, that slender-waisted woman was distressed.
In order to appease that sorrow, the goddess Arundhatī said: / 'I shall revive him this day with ash itself, O fair-smiling woman.'
Then she presented the ash born of the Agnihotra fire to Arundhatī; / with the Mṛtyuṃjaya mantra, she cast it upon the dead creature.
The fair-smiling woman produced a gentle breeze with a fan; / then that living creature arose through the power of this ash.
Then, when a hundred years had elapsed, one kinsman killed him. / When her husband died, that chaste and fair-smiling woman was grieving.
The chaste woman went for refuge to the eminent brāhmaṇa named Dadhīca, a sage who was a great devotee of Maheśvara; / the brāhmaṇa rich in asceticism said:
'Ash revived the treasure of asceticism Jamadagni when he was bereft of three lifespans, / and likewise Kaśyapa who was in such a state,
and the gods who had become thus, and even me in such a state in former times; / therefore, with ash I shall revive your creature, O sinless woman.'

Having spoken thus, the venerable Dadhīci went for refuge to Maheśvara;
then, consecrating ashes with mantras and taking them in hand, he revived the husband of that most virtuous woman.
From the touch of the hand of Maheśa, Karuṇa was freed from the curse; / and returning to his own form, he went to his own hermitage.
That chaste woman, having brought Dadhīca to her home, / begged the brāhmaṇa sage to dine; then that twice-born ate.
When the eminent twice-born had eaten, ten million disciples assembled; / then the gods arrived, their bodies smeared with ash.
Having bowed to Dadhīca, they inquired with a desire for Śiva: / The gods said: / 'Formerly our knowledge was lost, O broad-minded one!
Having seen the wife of Gautama, we were afflicted with passion; / and thus that lady, who had completed the auspicious rites of marriage, was violated.
And to us who desired her, our knowledge was lost; / then all of us, having become spirits, went to the sage Durvāsas.
He said: "Now I shall remove all your defilement; / it was consecrated with the Śatarudriya mantra by Śambhu himself,
and given even to me by him for the pacification of brāhmaṇa-murder and the like." / Having spoken thus, Durvāsas gave the supreme ash.
Then, by his word, all of us whose consciousness had been corrupted, / having had our bodies smeared with ash through the Śatarudriya mantra,
became completely cleansed of sin in that very moment. / We recognize this as a wonder, that the power of ash is such.'
Dadhīca said: / 'I shall tell you briefly the power of the ash of Śiva; / it would not be possible to declare it in detail even in hundreds of years.
In this regard I will recount to all of you an ancient event concerning the two gods / Hari and Śaṅkara, the destruction of brāhmaṇa-murder and other sins.
Long ago, when there was a dreadful cosmic dissolution into a single ocean during Brahmā's dissolution, / the venerable Mahāviṣṇu was sleeping on the waters of dissolution.
Reaching his two sides were two hundred cosmic eggs; / twenty were at the side of his feet, and twenty within his head.'
The Lord wore a universe as a nose-pearl; / in the circle of his navel some great sages, Lomaśa and others,
were practicing intense austerities and worshiping the Lord. / Then Viṣṇu, full of great splendour, fell into anxiety through a desire to create.
Absorbed in meditation and yoga, he saw nothing at all; / then, in great sorrow, he wept loudly again and again.
In the meantime, a certain radiance, extraordinary in all the worlds, [appeared]; / and having seen it, Hari closed both his eyes in fear.
A figure was approaching, whose splendour was like cow's milk, possessing a body, / who strung together in both hands a pair of garlands made of ten million universes,
bearing on his chest an abode fashioned from ten million universes, / while a single universe was falling down and springing up between his two hands,
endowed with every ornament—seeing that imperishable one in such a state, / Viṣṇu praised him indeed in order to behold him.
Viṣṇu said: / 'Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods! Homage to you, O eternal, imperishable one! / I do not know you, O Lord, but you know [me]; homage, homage!
Nor do I know your nature, and your splendour is hard to look upon. / [You wear] ruby earrings and are adorned with a web of gold garlands,
with a charming jewel ring, and ornaments on your arms and forearms, / with shining, wide eyes scattered over your slender, red, excellent [form],
with an imperishable eye on your forehead resembling a pointed arrow-eye, / the Lord whose eyebrows produce the illusion of the bow of the god of love,
with an oily, prominent, very handsome nose and clear cheeks, / gently smiling, with a joyful face, the omnipresent Lord who looks like the young moon,
wearing a red garment of wisdom, with ornaments fashioned from the Vedas. / I have taken refuge in you; grant me an eye, O omnipresent Lord!
Be a refuge to me, who am wretched, blind, miserable, and ruined by ignorance.' / Then he gave [him] a divine eye endowed with the power to see his own self.
Then Hari, seeing the three-eyed Śambhu standing before him, / said: 'Who are you?' Then: 'I do not know you, O one of great renown!
I am able only to offer bow, not to know [you].' / Sadāśiva said: / 'I shall grant you knowledge. First perform a bath in water,
and after that, a bath in ashes; then I shall impart knowledge.' / The holy Lord said: / 'Nowhere is there water fit for my bath.'

Thus addressed, he sat down, his body adhering to the cosmic egg;
water reaching up to the thighs was not suitable for Hari's bathing.
Śambhu laughed: 'Ah, the water for the bath is indeed exceedingly plentiful!' / Dadhīca said: / Then the god Śiva looked upon Viṣṇu with the eye on his forehead;
he looked with his left eye [at him], whose subtle limbs had dissolved. / Then Viṣṇu, having a subtle body and a cool form, was addressed by Śambhu:
'Bathe, O Viṣṇu! This pool has been created [for you].' / Then, when Hari [went] to bathe in the pool fashioned in Hara's lap,
he was unable to enter, because of the depth of that pool. / Hari said: 'There is no path to enter this pool.
Let a way be given to me, O god!' Śambhu then said to him: / 'Earlier, this vast water was ten million yojanas deep;
even while you were seated, O omnipresent one, the water reached only to your thighs. / How is it that now, even as you stand, there is no entry into the pool?
In that pool of mine, this thigh is eight finger-breadths in measure. / I am watching: do enter, and I will give you the touch of my feet.
My single utterance, the Veda issuing from my speech, is a stairway.' / Hari said: / 'No one here possesses the capacity to mount speech.
Grasping what is corporeal is possible, but how can one grasp Vedic scripture?' / Śambhu said: / 'A person does not have the capacity to hold, mount, or do the like with physical things.
Take this great Veda.' And then Hari took it. / His hands bowed down from weakness, Janārdana was as if falling,
and Hari said to Śiva: 'I am not able to hold it.' / Śiva, smiling, made him descend and brought him down into the great pool:
'Now climb that stairway, O Keśava, and you ought to bathe.' / Dadhīca said: / When the Veda indeed became a stairway reaching up to the thighs,
he bathed there according to rule, came out, and said: / 'I have bathed. What is to be done now?' Then Śambhu said to Hari:
'What do you meditate upon in your heart? Tell me: nothing?' / Hari said: 'Nothing.' Then Śambhu said to him:
'Completely purified by a bath in ashes, you will know the supreme good. / For that is recommended for an initiate; I shall perform that protection.'
Dadhīca said: / Śaṅkara took a portion of the ash resting on his own chest with a nail, / consecrated it with the praṇava and then with the Gāyatrī that has become Brahman,
and picking it up with two fingers, Śiva cast it with the five-syllable mantra / onto Hari's head and all his limbs.
Then, gazing with a peaceful glance, Hara said to Hari: 'Live! / Meditate: what is in your heart?' And he became intent on meditation.
He saw in his heart a lamp, elongated in form and intensely brilliant. / Hari said directly to Śiva: 'I have seen a lamp.'
Śiva said: 'Your knowledge is not yet fully ripened, O Hari. / Eat the ash; complete knowledge will come into being.'
Hari said: 'I shall eat the auspicious ash; formerly I was bathed with ash.' / Seeing the Lord accessible through devotion, Acyuta ate the ash.
Then a great wonder took place: having the splendour of a ripe bimba fruit, / Vāsudeva instantly took on the color of a pure pearl.
From then on, that Vāsudeva was white and serene. / Becoming intent on meditation again, [he saw] in the middle of the lamp a Puruṣa,
resembling pure crystal, three-eyed, two-armed, Śiva, / bestowing a boon with his right hand and offering fearlessness with his left, the omnipresent Lord,
having the body of a five-year-old, with the splendour of ten thousand autumn moons, / wearing ruby earrings and adorned with a web of gold garlands,
charming with a jewel ring, well adorned on his arms and forearms, / with slender red lips and wide eyes extending to his ears,
with an imperishable eye on your forehead resembling a pointed arrow-eye, / the Lord whose eyebrows produce the illusion of the bow of the god of love,
with an oily, prominent, very handsome nose and clear cheeks, / gently smiling, with a joyful face, the omnipresent Lord who looks like the young moon,
wearing a red garment of wisdom, with anklets fashioned from the Vedas, / resting in the midst of the left finger-ring, the imperishable, supreme praṇava.
Then Viṣṇu, having seen him, felt fulfilled at that time. / Then Śambhu said: 'O Viṣṇu, what was seen by you in your heart?'
Hari said: 'Previously a Puruṣa of peaceful form was seen.' / Having spoken thus, Mahāviṣṇu fell at Śiva's feet.
Hari said: 'I do not know the power of ash, or whence your majesty comes. / Homage to you! Homage to you! I have sought refuge in you alone.'
Sadāśiva said: / 'Choose a boon, O fortunate one, whatever you desire in your mind.' / Hearing Śiva's words, Hari chose an excellent boon.
Hari said: / 'O Śambhu, let there always be devotion in me to both your feet.' / Then, having granted the boon, Śambhu spoke this word to Hari:
'Endowed with the wearing of ashes, you will be my devotee.' / Dadhīca said: / 'Thus has the great knowledge arising from ash been told from the beginning.'

"Therefore, all you gods, wear it with reverence!"
And the gods, their eyes wide with wonder, said, "So be it."

Whoever hears this sacred narrative daily, supreme as it is,
is freed from all sins and goes to the realm of Śaṃkara.

5.106.m:
Dadhīca said:
In this regard I shall tell you an ancient legendary history,
which indeed became renowned between Citragupta and Yama.

Formerly in Mithilā, a certain dog was wandering out of hunger.
In the past, a hundred births ago, he had been a brāhmaṇa resolved upon sin.

In his earlier age, he was rich in Vedic learning, rich in the śāstras, and very intelligent.
He went to the Jāhnavī to bathe; and having bathed, he worshipped the ancestors,

the gods, and the sages, and went to the city of Prāttalikāpura.
Then he took shelter in the dwelling of a brāhmaṇa.

There was a certain daughter of a kṣatriya, in the prime of her youth, whose beloved was dead,
deprived of her kingdom, but possessing wealth amounting to sixty million niṣkas.

Then, as the brāhmaṇa, handsome in every limb, lay resting after eating,
at night, when the pure moon had risen and the moonlit directions were smiling,

she approached the brāhmaṇa, looked at him, and said:
"From where have you come, O vipra, and to which land will you go?"

The brāhmaṇa said:
"Inopportune conduct surely produces suspicion in everyone.
A conversation in private between two people in the prime of youth is a house of mockery here."

The kṣatriya woman said:
"In the course of conversation, on a journey, at a holy bathing place, during the ruin of a land or the like,
in famine, or when a village burns, a conversation in private is not considered a fault.

Moreover, you yourself formerly took shelter in my house,
and I am a resident of my house; there is no suspicion for anyone here."

The brāhmaṇa said:
"I must remain silent; you must go away at once."
Addressed thus by the brāhmaṇa, she thought in her mind:

"I must arrange things so that my union with him takes place.
I shall weep, and so he will come to comfort me;

and when he has come to comfort me, he will raise me up.
As I am being raised up, the creepers of my arms clinging to his neck,

touching his body with my pair of breasts, swooning—
seeing me deprived of consciousness, he will himself sit down,

and the foremost of the twice-born will place my body on his lap.
Then, as if unconscious, discarding my garment, and weeping,

I will show him that place—very smooth, hairless, shaped like a ripe leaf of the sacred fig tree,
the abode of desire, and fragrant.

As I roll upon him, his garment will fall away from his body;
and clinging to him, I will bring the twice-born under my control.

The mind is not the same before seeing as it is upon seeing;
and the mind is not the same upon seeing as it is through conversation.

The mind is not the same in conversation as it is in playful speech;
and the mind is not the same in playful speech as it is through touch.

The mind is not the same through touch as it is upon seeing the vulva;
and the mind is not the same upon seeing it as it is through touching the vulva.

From seeing and touching the armpits, the pair of breasts, and the vulva,
whose mind does not stumble, and whose semen is not discharged?
And when she had wept for a long time, the brāhmaṇa, an ocean of compassion,

[thought:] "The rescue from suffering of women, children, the elderly, the sick, kings, and ascetics,
from falling into poison, fire, water, off a mountain, and so forth, is praised; they say it is equal to the gift of a well."

Reflecting thus, that vipra, having purified himself, with a serene mind,
went near her, and then the twice-born said to her:

"Enough of this great grief, which is an obstacle both in this world and the next!
For this withers the body and destroys the mind.

Cast off this grief, child; there is indeed no benefit in lamenting.
What is the cause of the grief on account of which you weep in this way?"

Then the brāhmaṇa, who knew the highest truth, lifted her up;
raised and supported by him, she fell again and again.

As she fell again and again, the vipra sat down, raised her up again,
placed her on his lap, and wiped her eyes.

Then, as if fainting, she quickly removed her garment,
showing him her breasts, her secret parts, her armpits, and her eyes.

Clasping his neck with both arms, she touched the twice-born with her breasts.
And the moonlight was brilliant, and a gentle breeze arose.

Then the vipra was filled with anxiety: "This must not be done by me;
it is not proper for a father, a mother, a husband, or a teacher.

Since I am confounded, everything appears contrary to me."
Then Kama arrived as the two remained in secret;

Kama pierced the wicked-minded twice-born with sharp arrows.
Afflicted by the arrows of Smara, the lustful vipra reflected:

"This woman of lovely limbs appears to be a passionate lover;
otherwise, how could there be bristling of the hair at the entrance of her vulva?

Therefore, through the touch of her breasts, everything will become clear."
Having thought this in his mind, the twice-born touched her breasts and vulva.

She too, as if unconscious, had a gentle smile on her face;
she embraced the twice-born firmly and kissed his mouth.

Then their union lasted for even a hundred years.
When the hundred years had passed, afterwards on one day, the twice-born

went to the river in the morning to bathe; and she too, due to her attachment to the vipra,
bathed there in like manner. Then he heard the Purāṇa,

the Kūrma Purāṇa, which destroys all sins and grants devotion to Śiva;
and he heard this verse spoken by an expert in the Purāṇa:

"The slayer of a brāhmaṇa, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise the violator of the guru's bed—
merely by hearing the Kūrma Purāṇa, he is freed from that sin."

Hearing this statement, the vipra spoke to the reciter of the Purāṇa:
"There is no counting the sins committed by me;

from worshipping him, O vipra, all sin is destroyed.
Sin is called darkness; it is destroyed by the lamp of knowledge.

Or else, O vipra, through worship comes the destruction of all sins.
For those bereft of knowledge and worship, falling into hell is certain."

Dadhīca said:
Then the twice-born went to an excellent temple of Śiva,
and worshipped Śaṃkara with a thousand droṇa flowers.

Then he went home and took his meal;
and leaving the kṣatriya woman, the vipra went from there to a desirable land.

Taking sacrificial food, being unable to eat, he went to a temple of Śiva,
and ate outside using the ghee remaining in a lamp.

Then, having fallen under the power of death, he indeed went to the realm of Yama.
Yama said:
"Formerly there was destruction of some of the sins committed by you,"
"Because on one day you performed worship of Śaṅkara, / a thousand of your sins, O twice-born, have been destroyed.
Yet the fruit of the remaining sins is falling into hell / for twenty million years, O vipra, and then a hundred births as a dog.
From stealing the ghee of Śiva's lamp, the fruit is experiencing hell; / and his stay in hell will be very terrifying for a hundred years.
In Kumbhīpāka, becoming like firewood, reduced to ashes again and again / for a period of ten years; and then being food for worms for another ten;
and then being the wick of a lamp for ten years; / and in pools of phlegm, impure matter, excrement, urine, and semen,
emerging and submerging, then eating phlegm, feces, and filth; / then, by the remainder of hell, a hundred births as a dog thereafter."
Having heard this speech of Yama, the brāhmaṇa fell down. / Then his beloved wife became consumed with worry for her husband.
In the meantime, Nārada approached her. / Deeply sorrowful, she fell at Nārada's feet.
Lifting up that pure woman whose [husband's] life had ended, the sage spoke: / "O innocent one, large-eyed woman, you ought to go to your husband.
Indeed, O large-eyed woman, your husband has died, bereft of kin. / You should not weep, O good woman; enter the fire, O lady!"

The brāhmaṇa's wife said:
"Whether it is impossible or possible for me to go, tell me, O sage, / so that the time for entering the fire will indeed not pass by."

Nārada said:
"That town is indeed a hundred yojanas from this place. / Tomorrow, certainly, will be the vipra's cremation; you ought to go."

Avyayā said:
"How can I go to my husband, who is situated so far away, O sage?" / Hearing her words, Nārada spoke to her:
"Sit on the neck of my vīṇā, [and] I will go in an instant!" / Having said this, he went at that moment, made haste, and arrived at that
region, the place of the deceased twice-born. The sage said to Avyayā: / "Weeping should not be done here if you will enter the fire there.
If any sin has been committed, O good woman—the servicing of another man— / perform an expiation, O daughter, for the purification of this.
The destruction of your multitude of minor sins [comes] from entering the fire. / I see no other means for women to pacify all sins,

except for the single expiation of entering the fire in the three worlds."
Dadhīca said:
Then, impelled by Nārada's speech, she spoke these words:

"In entering the fire, what should be done by women, O great sage?"
Nārada said:
"Bathing, the auspicious ceremony, the wearing of ornaments and collyrium,
fragrant paste and flowers, likewise incense, the wearing of turmeric and unbroken grains, / and the auspicious thread, and indeed lac-dye on the feet;
giving according to one's means, pleasant speech, and a cheerful face; / and listening to various auspicious musical instruments and singing.
When a sin is committed through adultery, for the pacification of that sin, / having reached a past transgression, that expiation is declared [effective].
She should then make [ready] her own ornaments and bestow them upon a vipra. / In the absence of ornaments, she should indeed have the expiation performed with her own [means].

Otherwise, no destruction of that sin is known anywhere."
Avyayā said:
"I will do all this, [yet] no turmeric is found with me,

much less an ornament, O holy one! Let all this be granted [to me]."
Nārada said:
"There is no article of good fortune other than what you require."

Dadhīca said:
Then in an instant he went to Kailāsa, the dwelling of Śiva. / Then, seeing the Mountain-born Goddess, he bowed down and spoke thus:

"Let turmeric, ornaments, and the thread be given, O Mother!"
Pārvatī said:
"How can any ornament be given by me to a widow?

For when it has been given by me, widowhood cannot indeed occur."
Nārada said:
"O Mother, a woman is not a widow as long as her husband's body exists.

Until the cremation, there is no impurity; the highest good fortune remains."
Pārvatī said:
"And no other body is fit to wear my ornaments and turmeric.
When ornaments and the like are given by me, a long life is desired. / Indeed, let all this that was spoken by you be given by Jayantī alone."
Then he went to Jayantī; and what was given by her, he then brought. / The sage gave the turmeric to Avyayā as she was bathing.
Then the sage gave fine garments and ornaments. / And he said to her: 'Who will perform your funeral rites? Appoint him.'

Avyayā said:
"By you alone is the cause of all my rites, O sage! / You are my father; perform everything today! Homage to you, O best of sages!"

Dadhīca said:
Then, having cremated that brāhmaṇa, Nārada spoke to her: / "O Avyayā, go! Enter the fire if you wish."
Then, having adorned herself, that virtuous, fair-limbed woman, having first circumambulated three times / and bowed down to Nārada, fixing her mind [on him],
the very fine auspicious thread, turmeric, unbroken grains, / flowers, garments, musk, and sandalwood,
a golden comb, and various fruits— / having touched each separately with the end of her own garment and gifts,
she, desiring to please Pārvatī, gave everything to the married women. / And [approaching] the fire, which was burning the sky as if with garlands of flames,
having walked three times clockwise around it, standing before the fire, the faithful wife, / with folded hands and a smiling face, then spoke these words:

Avyayā said:
"O guardians of the directions headed by Indra, O Mother Earth, O Sun, / O all gods headed by Dharma, listen to my words!
If, beginning from the taking of my hand [in marriage] until this end, day and night, / my husband was served with devotion through speech, mind, and actions;
if no adultery occurred for me in the three stages [of life], / by that truth, grant me a journey together with my husband!"

Having spoken thus, she swiftly cast away the Puṣpaka [flower] from the tip of her hand;
having entered the blazing fire, she then beheld an aerial chariot.
exalted like the sun and adorned with the singing of apsarases. / She climbed onto the aerial chariot and went to heaven together with her husband.
Then Yama, having honored that woman devoted to her husband, said: / "Indeed, here is imperishable heaven for you, and you have no sin.
The sin for which there was a stay of twenty million years in hell, alas, / is wiped away without doubt. However, there is one sin
acquired by eating the ghee of Śiva's lamp: / falling into the ninth hell and a hundred births as a dog will take place."

Avyayā said:
"How can there be hell again for those purified by entering the fire? / From entering the fire, the destruction of all sins occurs."

Yama said:
"The sin of stealing the property of Śiva does not perish at all; / thus spoke Śambhu formerly. That of others may be destroyed."
Then he, having attained the state of a dog for a hundred years, after that, / reached the dwelling of Dadhīca and went into the jaws of death.
Near his wall, however, there lay consecrated ashes. / The dog fell onto the ashes, died, and went to Yama.
Yama, bowing low after honoring him, [said:] "You are a most holy sage. / A place in my house is not suitable for you; go outside!"
Then, having gone outside, that dog remained as told by Yama; / and Nārada saw him standing in distress.
And he asked: “Why are you standing here, full of radiance? / I know you are a devotee of Śiva who died lying on Śiva’s ashes, O wise one.
Even for sinners devoted to Śiva who take their lives by reckless acts, / there is no world of Yama; such is the command of Śiva proclaimed by Śiva.”
Dadhīca said: / Having addressed the dog thus, the sage went to Kailāsa. / Bowing like a staff before the Lord, he reported to Hara:
“O God, a certain dog is staying outside the city of Yama. / He died in the ashes; therefore he deserves the world of Bhava.”
Then Vīrabhadra, accompanied by leading attendants and directed by Śiva, / brought that dog, who then possessed a celestial form.
Bowing at the feet of Maheśa, he petitioned the God: / “Make me an attendant belonging to the Lord Maheśvara!”
Śiva said, “So be it,” and he became an attendant with the face of a dog. / Dadhīca said: The peerless greatness of ash has thus been told to you by me, O fair-smiling one.
Beyond this, what further do you wish to hear, O lady of noble vows?

5.107.m: Śucismitā said: / How did the ash once protect Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, / and the gods? Explain that to me, O sage, O holy one!
Dadhīca said: / Formerly, the gods accompanied by Kaśyapa and others came to a mountain / celebrated by the name Śokara, exceedingly beautiful in the midst of the ranges,
abounding with various birds, a refuge of various assemblies of sages, / a delight supported by Vāsudeva, frequented by troops of apsarases,
covered with diverse trees, resplendent with blossoms of every season. / Having entered such a mountain, we, together with others,
went there praising Keśava, the Lord of the mountain's master. / Seeing a great flame there, we stepped right into it.
Passing me by alone, it burned the deities and the sages; / afterwards it burned me, and we were turned to ashes, O auspicious lady.
Seeing us in that condition, the glorious Vīrabhadra, / for some reason or other, arrived at that mountain.
His whole body dusted with ashes, Śiva residing upon his head, pure, / solitary, desireless, and tranquil, he then heard a wailing cry.
Then he became filled with concern: “The sound of dying corpses / and the smell like that of corpses is perceived upon inspecting it.”

Having resolved thus in his mind, he approached the intensely radiant fire;
then that fire began to burn Vīrabhadra.
Like a fire of grass coming upon water, it became extinguished. / Then Vīrabhadra beheld another great flame,
a great dark flame traversing the sky and falling down as well. / And the glorious Vīrabhadra thought in his mind:
“This flame is destructive of all creatures by the hundreds of millions. / Indeed, to protect all of them, I, being thirsty, will
drink up this great flame as a thirsty man drinks water.” / In that interval, a bodiless voice addressed the hero.
Bhāratī said: / “O hero, do not commit a reckless deed! Where is thirst and where is fire? / For the thirsty, water is the objective; a forest fire is the very opposite.
A lord of rākṣasas whose head was a whole yojana in size perished, / and another with a mouth of a hundred yojanas and a hundred arms.
And the illustrious Agastya, who drank the ocean completely— / this flame has slain these and countless others.”
Vīrabhadra said: / “This terrible great flame mentioned by you will not come to be; / and O Sarasvatī, my anger is rising towards you.
Know me to be Vīrabhadra, whose feet are worshipped by all the gods.” / Bhāratī said: “I spoke out of good will, not out of enmity, nor otherwise, O sage.
Cast off your anger, O hero, and act for your own welfare!” / Having spoken thus, goddess Bhāratī vanished out of fear of the hero.
Then the hero simply with ease drank up that great flame. / In an instant, that huge flame extending a hundred yojanas
was swallowed by Vīrabhadra alone, though exceedingly difficult to endure. / Then heaps of ashes belonging to the sages headed by Indra
were seen by Vīrabhadra, and called upon by the high-souled one; / but they gave no reply, dead as those sages and deities were.
Vīrabhadra, discerning the destruction of the sages and deities, / pondered: “How may I, skilled as I am, revive them all today?”
And through meditation he perceived life in the bodies of ash. / Then, sipping water, he consecrated the ashes of the dead with ash,
using the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra. / Thereupon the excellent sages arose, assuming each their own form.
Then they proceeded to the side of that glorious mountain. / There too they were all devoured by a serpent of immense body.
Then the powerful hero approached the great serpent. / Seeing that the hero had arrived, the serpent began to fight.
The hooded serpent, assuming diverse forms, fought for a whole year. / Then the hero, seizing both its lips with his two hands,
tore its whole body in two. Seeing the gods there whose lives had departed, / Śaṅkara revived them with ash alone.
Then the gods together with the sages, bowing to Vīrabhadra, / went along the path and saw an approaching rākṣasa
who had five phalluses, an enormous body, ten arms, / five legs, and eight heads,
seeking a huge meal while fighting against Vālin. / Whatever strength Vāsudeva possessed in the form of the Great Boar,
that was certainly doubled in the monkey Vālin. / Against such a foremost monkey, along with Sugrīva, that rākṣasa
in a boxing match swiftly struck down Vālin with his five legs, / and proceeded with his hands to slay Sugrīva.
Throwing Sugrīva into his mouth, he swallowed him like a morsel of food. / Seeing the devouring of Vālin and Sugrīva, he became filled with concern:
“How shall I kill this one? How shall I protect the monkey?” / While he was thus contemplating that monkey, the lord of rākṣasas
swallowed him in a single effort. Seeing the rākṣasa in such a state, / all the divine sages were intent upon flight.
Seeing them fleeing, that rākṣasa with five phalluses / seized all of them with all his hands and devoured them then.
Then, seeing the devouring of the monkeys, sages, and gods, Vīrabhadra / took a rock of fifty yojanas in his hand in fury,
and struck him in the middle of his heads, and his middle head fell. / Then, seizing a hundred-yojana peak of the mountain
and setting it down very firmly, he struck the lord of rākṣasas thus. / Then the rākṣasa spoke to that three-eyed Vīrabhadra:
“Look at the strength of my arms; your strength has been witnessed by me! / Here are two oil-cleaned swords, fifty yojanas tall
and one yojana wide, very solid, endowed with auspicious marks. / Take one desirable and superior sword; it is dear to me.”
Vīrabhadra said, “So be it,” and taking the sword, the mighty one / brandished the sharp blade with his hand, and in anger roared a battle cry.
Sword in hand, the eminent rākṣasa likewise uttered a battle cry, / and rushing against Vīrabhadra, struck at his throat.
His body was pierced, and much blood flowed forth; / but the rākṣasa drank that blood with one hand.
In anger, Vīrabhadra struck the rākṣasa in the throat; / two heads were thus severed, and as they fell he seized them.
The immeasurable one devoured them and uttered a lion's roar; / by that mighty roar, the three worlds were shaken.
With bodies broken by each other's sword blows, opened wide, / they looked like two blossoming kiṃśuka trees drenched in blood.
Fighting with swords for one whole year, god and demon battled then; / after that, a fight with clubs took place between the two for one year.
Thereafter, the battle went on for one year with daggers; / seizing a pair of swords once again, they fought each other.
Lifting his great sword, the leader of the gaṇas, fanged in appearance, / his eyes red with fury, swung his sword forward.
He severed the entire forest of the demon's necks, as if cutting plantain trees; / seizing all the heads, the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes devoured them.
Tearing the demon's body open with his claws, he drew forth the gods, / the two monkey kings, and the others, and beheld the Supreme Goddess.
Having witnessed this most terrifying battle, Nārada approached / and informed Brahmā, Vāsudeva, and Śaṅkara:
“The sages and the gods have been preserved, as have the two monkeys, Vālin and Sugrīva.” / The one whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva then revived them.
A boon of an exceedingly harsh nature had been granted to the rākṣasa by Śambhu: / in the kingdom of Hiraṇyakaśipu, there was a single powerful rākṣasa.
He fought together with the gods for a wondrous hundred years; / the gods fled in many directions, and hundreds of them perished.
Protected then by his teacher Śukra, he reflected: / “I have died hundreds of times, O Śukra, and by you alone have I been revived.
Grant me immunity from death caused by this, and death to one who enters my belly; / otherwise, death will come to me, of this there is no doubt.
O teacher, there was a terrible battle between me and Yama; / I swallowed that powerful king Yama in the battle.
Entering my belly, he tore it open and roared; / I died then, and was revived once more by you.
Therefore, I will perform austerities for the death of those who abide in my belly.” / Śukra said: “It is so, there is no doubt; proceed as is fitting.
There is the sacred place Syamantapañcaka; you ought to perform austerities there.” / The rākṣasa said: “I will perform a great and terrible austerity, such as was never practiced by gods or demons.
Having bound my feet at the ankles with iron fetters, / and having erected two iron pillars fitted with an iron bar,
and tying my feet to the bar so as to hang head downward, / keeping my mouth wide open and facing down from above,
above the pillars, in the fire, in the circle of flames on all sides, / standing head downward, keeping my eyes wide open—
in this way I will perform austerities. May someone become the granter of my boon; / let the granter of the boon be Brahmā, Śaṅkara, or Viṣṇu.
I must have a granter of boons, whoever that boon-giver may be.” / Thus spoken to by the sage, his teacher Bhārgava,
he performed austerities for six months, and then he did something further: / cutting off his own head with his nails, he offered it into the fire with a mantra.
With the mantra “homage to Bhadra,” he offered four heads; / and as the rākṣasa was striving to surrender the fifth head,
from the middle of the fire arose the blessed Lord, the husband of Ambikā, / resembling pure crystal, adorned with the crescent moon.
Maheśvara said this to that rākṣasa who was hanging head downward: / “Do not commit rashness, O rākṣasa! I am the granter of boons; choose a boon.”
The rākṣasa said: “You are indeed the giver of many boons, O Maheśvara. / Let there be regrowth of severed heads, and death to the living swallowed by me.
Let my strength be four times that of Viṣṇu in his boar form; / let there be anger toward him by me, and let him always be in my presence.
Let a single person arise from the tearing out of your matted hair; / let my death be at his hands alone, and not by others—let this be chosen by me.”
Hara vanished after saying, “It shall be exactly so.” / Thus that wicked rākṣasa, having obtained this boon, was slain by you.
Then, having embraced the hero, Hari, Śaṅkara, and the Grandfather / departed just as they had come; then the wives of the gods and others,
prostrating themselves like a staff upon the ground, said to Vīrabhadra: / “Homage to you, O Lord of the gods! Homage to you, O maker of compassion!
Homage to you, O eternal, endless one! Homage to you; be the granter of our wish!” / Vīrabhadra said: “With sacred ash I will revive the gods along with the sages and the monkeys.
You women should be comforted; no grief should be felt now.” / Having spoken thus, Vīrabhadra revived them with sacred ash.
The sages and the gods arose, and the two monkeys arose then; / delighted, folding their hands above their heads, bowing, they spoke these words:
“We have been restored to life by you, O father; in righteousness you are our father. / Be our eternal refuge, O born of Śaṅkara!
Seeing the wicked deeds of children, you would instruct them; / you would protect them from afflictions caused by others and from diseases, like one's own offspring.
Having committed offenses at Dakṣa's sacrifice, we were instructed by you, O sinless one; / now we have been protected, O father, like your own children.”
Vīrabhadra said: “This is true, there is no doubt; wherever affliction should befall you, / remember me there swiftly, and the affliction will vanish.
Those who recite the name ‘Vīrabhadra’ one hundred and eight times, / preceded by the praṇava, ending with namaḥ, and joined with the dative case,
for them there will be the destruction of afflictions caused by rākṣasas, / in torments by brahmarākṣasas, and in fears of piśācas and the like.
From remembering the name, all afflictions are destroyed:

‘The fierce Lord, whose eyes have the brilliance of lightning, whose lower lip is adorned with fangs red like the young moon, / whose body is deep black, who wears a garland of matted hair, and bears the tripuṇḍra of ash upon his body.’
This remembrance has been declared for deliverance from brahmarākṣasas; / and all this has been declared in the mantra of Vīrabhadra.”
Dadhīca said: “Then the hero did thus; the sages and the gods departed. / This excellent glorification of the ash called ‘Triyāyuṣa’ has been proclaimed.
It destroys sins for one who reads it, hears it, or remembers it; / it bestows devotion to Śiva, is meritorious, and increases lifespan and health.”
Śucismitā said: “I have accomplished my goal, I am fortunate, and I am the best among women; / my sins have been destroyed. Homage to you, O best of sages!”

5.108.m: Glorious Rāma said: “Speak to me, O highly fortunate one, of the origin of ash, the glorification of ash, / the merit in applying ash, and in the giving of ash.”
Śambhu said: “I shall proclaim the origin of ash, which destroys all sins / through remembrance and recitation; listen to it, O Rāma, O ruler of men!
The one eternal God, praised by Brahmā, is Sadāśiva, / the three-eyed, the substratum of the guṇas, beyond the guṇas, imperishable, and unchanging.
The desire to create arose in him when he observed the three guṇas residing within himself; / this triad of the Vedas should be known to be indeed this triad of guṇas.
Separating [the qualities] from himself, dear one, and dividing the places there, / from his right side he created a son, Brahmā, and from his left side Hari,
and on his back the all-pervading lord created Maheśāna—three sons. / As soon as they were born, the three gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
spoke these clear words: 'Who are you, and who are we?' / Śiva said to those sons: 'You are my sons, and I am your father.
Sons, take up these three qualities, which are the cause of action.' / The sons said: / 'Which quality should be taken up by whom, and for how long, O Lord?
And how does the cessation of the qualities occur? Tell us this.' / Śiva said: 'As long as your knowledge lasts, or indeed as long as your lifespan,
for just so long shall be the holding of each quality: / Brahmā should take up sattva, Viṣṇu rajas, and Maheśvara tamas.'

The moment this was spoken by the lord of the gods, Brahmā seized that substance;
he was unable even to move it, so how could he be capable of bearing it?

Discarding that quality, he then took up the quality of rajas; / unable even to move it, he then seized the quality of tamas.

Unable even to move it, he fell down and wept. / Viṣṇu held the quality of rajas with his left hand,
and Maheśa held the quality of tamas with two fingers. / Then, [lifting] sattva alone with his fingers, [Śiva] placed sattva and Viṣṇu,
and Brahmā upon his footstool, and he danced.
Dancing, possessing a form of supreme charm, appearing like cow's milk, youthful, three-eyed, / bearing all, creating wonder—beholding him, Śiva, the giver of boons, spoke to his sons.
Śiva said: 'My son, I am pleased with you; choose a boon as you desire.' / Then the son said to the father: 'Grant me this boon:
May worship performed towards me become worship to you, O Śiva; / and may you always dwell in me, and may you be me, O imperishable one.'
Śiva said: 'So it shall be, O fortunate one; of this there is no doubt. / These two sons, red and pale, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, belong only to me;
and the hairs at the base of my arms have my form, sinless ones.' / Then he said this to Brahmā: 'You take up one quality.'
Brahmā said: 'I am indeed not able to bear the quality indicated by you, O Lord; / I shall bear rajas, O god; let Hari take up sattva,
and the remaining quality this Īśvara will bear.' / Śambhu said: 'Taking up the qualities, those gods were unable to bear them permanently.
In order to acquire the power of bearing [them], he spoke again to Śiva: / 'We are not able to bear the qualities at all times.
Let power be given, O Blessed One, if you are a giver of boons.' / Then, hearing those words, Śiva spoke these words:
Śiva said: 'The power of all is named the power of knowledge. / Knowledge rests on the three qualities, and ignorance rests on them as well.
Having burned the three qualities, you are worthy to hold their essence; / whatever may be there, let that be borne by you.'
Then his sons spoke these words: 'There is no burning without fire.' / Śiva said: 'There is indeed fire in the eye of Maheśa.
These three qualities are the cow; the auspicious dung is knowledge; / and the urine is declared to be the Upaniṣad; after that one should make the ash.
Its calves are the Smṛtis, from which cow dung is produced. / With the mantra "ā gāvaḥ" one should consecrate the cow there.
With "gāvo gāvo gāvaḥ" one should feed grass and water [to it]. / Having fasted on the fourteenth day of either the bright or the dark [fortnight], the observer of the vow,
rising early on the next day, purified and composed, / having bathed and wearing washed clothes, should go to the cow for the sake of the dung.
Raising her with care, one should collect the urine with the Gāyatrī. / One should place it in a gold, silver, copper, or earthen jar,
or in a vessel of lotus wood, or of palāśa, or in a cow's horn; / one should indeed hold the cow urine, and take the cow dung with the mantra "gandhadvārām".
One should catch it before it falls to the ground in the vessel described above. / A wise man should purify the cow dung with the mantra "śrīr me bhajatu".
Wiping the cow dung is done with the mantra "alakṣmīr me". / With the mantra "saṃ tvā siñcāmi", one should pour the cow urine onto the cow dung.
With the mantra "pañcānāṃ tvā", one should make fourteen balls; / having dried them in the rays of the sun, one should collect them.
Then one should place the cow dung balls in the vessel described before; / having established the fire according to the rule declared in one's own Gṛhyasūtra, one should kindle it.

One should throw the balls into the fire, dedicating the balls to the respective deity of the syllable. / The wise man, having poured the two libations and the two portions of clarified butter, should offer oblations,
and then to the lord of death, thirteen offerings beginning with Jayā; / the five Brahmans should be offered to with "namo hiraṇyabāhave".

Thus having offered all the oblations with mantras ending in the dative case,
then to Śarva, to Rudra, and [with the verse] "Whose is the vaikaṅkata [wood]..."
with these the learned man should make offerings, and likewise [with] the three anājñāta [mantras]. / Then having offered the vyāhṛtis, he should then sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Having completed the remainder of the fuel, he should then swell / the water of the full vessel with other water, using the Yajus formula ending in pūrṇamāsa.
With ‘In the brāhmaṇas is nectar,’ he should pour that water upon his head. / With the markers of the quarters, ‘In the east,’ he should cast water in the directions.
Having given a sacrificial fee to the Brahman priest, he should fetch chaff when it is cooled: / ‘I will fetch [it] for the protection of the rites of all the gods;
O Jātavedas, for the restraint of mortals, cover with chaff today!’ / With this mantra, he should then cover that fire with chaff.
Covering with chaff is prescribed for keeping the fire burning for three days. / With devotion he should feed brāhmaṇas; he himself should eat restraining his speech.
Desiring abundant ash, however, he should take more cow dung, / whether across three days or in a large amount in a single day.
On either the third or fourth [day], having bathed in the morning, clad in white garments, / wearing a white sacrificial thread, smeared with white ointments and wearing white garlands,
with clean teeth, smeared with ash, the knower of mantras, with this mantra: / Having uttered ‘tadvetti’, he must not abandon the true ash.
Then the sixteen services of worship, beginning with invocation, / are to be performed with offerings; then he should withdraw the fire.
With the mantra ‘agne bhasma’, he should take the produced ash. / And with the mantra ‘agnir asmi’, having wiped it after that,
combining it with Gaṅgā water or with milk from a Kapila cow, / camphor, saffron, Kashmirian [crocus], uśīra root, sandalwood,
and both kinds of agallochum—having finely powdered them, / he should cast that powder into the ash with the Praṇava, from the Brahman mantra.
Then, for sprinkling the milk, the formula for the Kapila cow is recited: / ‘Nectar is your milk, O goddess, sacred and thriving here.
By your grace, mortals are freed from all sin.’ / The wise man should then fashion balls of ash with the Praṇava,
with the mantra ‘aṇor aṇīyān’, discerningly. / Śambhu said: Having thus prepared the ash and taking it dry, the knower of mantras,
having wiped it with the Praṇava and consecrated it seven times with the Praṇava, / [should consecrate] the region of the head with Īśāna, and the face with Tatpuruṣa,
the chest region with Aghora, the private parts he should consecrate with Vāmadeva, / the feet with Sadyojāta, and the whole body with the Praṇava.
Then, having dusted his whole body with ash from the soles of the feet to the head, / having then sipped water, he should put on clean white clothing.
Having sipped water again, he is fully fit to perform his own rites. / Then, taking ash and wiping it with the Praṇava,
remembering the three-eyed Lord, the support of the three guṇas, father of the three, / with ‘Salutations to Śiva,’ [he should make] a tripuṇḍra on his forehead.
Saying ‘Salutations to both Śivās,’ a tripuṇḍra on both arms as well; / ‘Salutations to Aghora’ on both forearms;
then with ‘To Bhīma’ on the back, and likewise on the western part of the head; / with ‘To Nīlakaṇṭha’ he should cast [ash] on his head, [saying] ‘Salutations to the Universal Self.’
Then, having washed both hands, he should carry out the ritual practice. / Śiva said: ‘You, in this manner, having made ash and rubbed it,
are able to bear the guṇas; then you will indeed create offspring.’ / Śambhu said: Thus addressed by Śiva, the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
having done so according to the rules, in mutual rivalry at that time, / unable to instruct one another, bowed and said to Śiva:
‘Who should bear what guṇa?’ Then Śiva said to his sons: / ‘Power of action and likewise knowledge perish solely through the dust of the mouth.
Brahmā is seen to be short-lived, and his lifespan is measured by Manus. / I who am adorned with garlands of cosmic eggs am the protector of the Brahman.
Relying on the quality of rajas, you did not know me then. / Viṣṇu has greater power than Brahmā, superior to Brahmā in lifespan.
When I, Maheśa, am adorned with garlands of cosmic eggs, / Viṣṇu’s lifespan is declared to be the span of just four exhalations.
Because of having more sattva than Brahmā, let Hari take refuge in sattva. / He knows me at all times; never at all does he forget me.
Only sāttvika worship should be done, not rājasika or tāmasika. / The peaceful, auspicious sattva quality, through disrespect of the mouth of rajas,
and likewise the sky-blue quality, Śambhu embraced. / Indeed, long ago he bore sattva, rajas, and tamas as well.
Therefore, various kinds of worship are prescribed for this Śaṅkara. / Rajas joined with tamas is declared to be dreadful;
even dreadful worship of Śaṅkara is considered to grant a good state. / Rajas joined with tamas is an impurity that sets the treatises in motion;
even interrupted worship of Śaṅkara is considered to bear fruit. / And tamas combined with sattva is mixed and active;
mixed worship too bears fruit in Śaṅkara, who brings welfare to the world. / Whatever kind of worship of the Lord is performed with regularity,
it swiftly yields fruit for Śaṅkara, for whatever kind of embodied being.’ / Śambhu said: This procedure of the ash has been told in brief, O sinless one,
destroying all sins of those who speak it and those who hear it.

5.109.m: Śambhu said: Here I will relate to you a story that destroys sin, / upon hearing which the righteous-minded one attained supreme devotion to Śiva.
There was an eminent brāhmaṇa named Ikṣvāku, highly learned and greatly wise, / proficient in many sciences and skilled in the treatises on statecraft.
He was neither a sacrificer nor a giver of gifts, nor a worshipper of the gods, / nor a teacher of the Veda, nor an expounder of what was heard,
nor of the Purāṇas, histories, revelations, or sacred scriptures; / he was intent on eating with effort, solely devoted to the bodily embellishment.
As he lived in such a way, the lifespan of this twice-born one reached a hundred thousand [years]. / After that hundred thousand, in one year, in the fifth month,
on the third day, at night, he heard this Purāṇa: / ‘Whoever makes no gift from wealth acquired by himself,
it will gradually become devoid of essence as it is consumed day by day. / For just as many years he is surely cooked in hell.
And having experienced a thousand births as a worm after that, / [he is born] poor, diseased, friendless, with a wicked wife and many offspring,
living day by day by begging and asking for alms; / or, searching for seeds submerged wherever,
living on what is obtained, living the life of hired servants, / bereft of hearing in between, blind, dropping feces.’
Having heard this Purāṇa, that Ikṣvāku, extremely sorrowful, / remembering it again and again, that lowest of the twice-born thought this in his mind:
‘Even an inaccessible buffalo-cow adorned with beautiful flowers is without fruit; / so too knowledge devoid of the Purāṇas does not show the true path.
Having studied many sciences and many Vedas in full detail, / the insight of a man who has not heard the Purāṇa never reaches completion.’
Śambhu said: As he was thinking thus, his untimely death occurred. / And having gone to the realm of Yama, he was addressed by Yama:

Yama said:
You are bound up with manifold sins, and your merit is not at all great; / nor did you know the sin incurred from teaching the Veda [for gain].
O twice-born, your stay in hell is for millions of years. / Your life is very short; return to your former body.
Perform merit, beneficial gift-giving, worship of deities, and recitation of mantras; / teaching [the Veda] with its limbs, feeding brāhmaṇas, and applying sacred ash.
Worship the divine Lord of the Universe, the God of gods, the husband of Umā. / By mere effort toward Him, you will not come to my realm.
O sinner, listen daily with reverence to even a little Purāṇa; / then, through that hearing alone, you will not see my torments.
Having heard Yama's words, the brāhmaṇa returned to his own body. / Then, relying on effort for the worship of the Lord, that twice-born man
went to the foremost of sages, Jābāli, the worshipper of Śiva, / who was endowed with austerities and Vedic recitation, a discerner of Śruti and Smṛti,
a knower of the truth of the Purāṇas, surrounded by a hundred thousand disciples, / his limbs all withered by old age, one who had crossed over the Veda and the Vedāṅgas.
Desiring to see [him], he went to Mount Mandara with its lovely caves, / full of various birds and covered with diverse flowering creepers,
endowed with flowers of all seasons, adorned with various fragrances, / its great caves filled with the songs of pairs of Kinnaras;
its trees inhabited by women of manifold beauty and charm, / its trees adorned by those women hanging down with variegated luster;
where bees awaken those asleep from the fatigue of lovemaking, / and cuckoos coo at will, indeed uniting separated lovers;
crowded with hosts of various sages, with tranquil deer roaming, / thronged with hosts of Apsarases, frequented by hosts of Gandharvas;
its inner forests filled with songs issuing from the mouths of diverse Siddhas, / full of wondrous fruits, endowed with temples of various deities;
congested with hundreds of palaces, endowed with various dwellings; / then with [lords of attendants] whose faces are like lions, elephants, and owls;
with faceless ones, averted-faced ones, fierce ones, half-faced ones, doe-faced ones, / and even those with the faces of ruru-deer, jantu-deer, lizards, snakes, monkeys, and bears;

with the snouts of tigers, scorpions, bears, camels, dogs, and donkeys; / with lords of Gaṇas whose countenances resemble the faces of all living creatures; / with creepers for faces, trees for faces, stone-faced, iron-faced;
adorned with faces resembling conches, pearls, and other water-born things; / with extra limbs, with limbless bodies, matted-haired, and crest-shaven;
bird-faced, twelve-faced, and with faces of threefold forms; / with faces like bells, winnowing baskets, ears, and feet;
with faces like bells, flutes, and tiny bells; / with faces like iron, resembling whatever objects exist in the world;
some tender with the beauty and charm of suppressed desire, / resembling millions of suns, equal in radiance to millions of moons;
of various colors, having universal faces, having universal forms, four-faced, / two-faced, five-faced, three-faced, and six-faced;
having one face or many faces, peaceful, always endowed with happiness, / abundant in diverse enjoyments, and equal to Rati and Kāma;
having faces like Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, having bodies equal to Umā and Īśa, / and by others bearing diverse forms, Mount Mandara was served;
where the Vedas are cows accompanied by the Mīmāṃsā calves, / where Dharma and the others have bodies, and the Purāṇas have action;
where the classes of Smṛti, Itihāsa, and the Āgamas dwell embodied / on Mandara—that mountain destroys sin.
In its middle is a most sacred, exquisitely adorned city, / adorned with hundreds of reservoirs, ponds, gardens, and palaces;
having seven ramparts and moats, furnished with jeweled turrets, / endowed with nine gateway-towers and variegated dwellings;
whose splendor is incomparable, free from heat, cold, and the like. / In its center is a sacred city, and in its center is an auspicious assembly hall.
In it, in the center, is a throne adorned with the Vedas for feet, / a most beautiful footstool fashioned from all the Upaniṣads.
The Purāṇas and Āgamas proclaim 'Svasti!' at the feet of Śiva. / Seated there is the great Yogin whose form resembles cow's milk;
a gentle smile on his very lovely face, the Lord sixteen years of age, / wearing a garland on his chest fashioned of gems and rudrākṣas;
wearing a sacred thread, radiant like the karṇikāra flower, / the God with fine jeweled earrings, a crown, and golden garments;
adorned with various ornaments, anointed with various perfumes, / having the Mountain's Daughter placed on his left lap, looking at her face;
she, an innocent, fair-faced maiden adorned with fresh youth, / her lovely whole body decorated, holding a golden lotus;
the God embracing the goddess with his left arm, lifting up her face with his right, / touching her head with his left hand, and applying a tilaka with his right.
Bhakti fans the God with the fan of the Praṇava; / Pūjā, his beloved, also holds a garland of flowers for the God;
Knowledge and Detachment, two women, hold the fly-whisks of yoga; / Samādhi is his man of affairs, and Dhāraṇā is his woman;
The Yamas and Niyamas are declared to be his servants; / Prāṇāyāma is the family priest, and Pratyāhāra holds the gold;
Dhyāna is the superintendent of wealth, and Truth is the commander-in-chief; / the bound creatures extend from Brahmā down to insects, and their lord is Śiva.
Dharma is the protector of the creatures, and Adharma is the thief; / they are bound by the cord of Māyā; death in Kāśī is the liberator.
Diverse women [attend] the God of gods, the husband of Umā. / If an individual soul recalls such a Lord of Umā amidst millions [of existences],
