having attained desired enjoyments, he is honored in the realm of Śiva. / Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and others are the gatekeepers of his city;
the goddesses Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are appointed to view the worship of the threshold and grounds / of the God of gods, and the gods and divine women [serve as attendants];
all gods are the female servants and male servants of that great-souled one. / Such a great mountain Ikṣvāku indeed saw.
Bowing down to the sage Jābāli, he then spoke this word: / 'Desiring to go to the great mountain, am I capable of it, O sage?'
'My life was declared by the all-knowing Yama to be short long ago,'
'and a great hell was proclaimed [for me]. How will welfare come to be?' / Jābāli said: 'All this has been known by me too through the divine eye.'
'Your lifespan is ten days, O brāhmaṇa; though learned, you did not practice dharma. / There is no austerity for you due to lack of practice, nor is there yoga due to the short time.'
'There is no gift-giving due to lack of wealth, nor worship due to inability; / there is no sacrifice, no vow, no public works, and no merit for one lacking longevity.'
'Nor is there teaching or serving holy places and the like, due to the contradiction of time. / Therefore, for the destruction of that sin, no expiation exists.'
'Whether granting a [good] destiny or dharma, go or stay, O sage.' / Ikṣvāku said: 'Whatever dharma is performed having made a vow for as long as one lives, O twice-born,'
'by that, the removal of sin will certainly take place. / Tell me that dharma by which my sin will be destroyed,'
'or by what conjunction of merit will there be a heavenly destiny? / Be a refuge, O brāhmaṇa sage, to one terrified of hell!'
'They declare protecting one who has taken refuge to be the fruit of all dharma.' / Jābāli said: 'True, but in a very short time such dharma is not obtained.'
even in nectar or untruth, it can be spoken in dreams as well; / but a certain secret is not told to just anyone.
Ikṣvāku said: / Save me, who have taken refuge, O sage; my time is going to run out. / Jābāli said: / Dearer to me than life, O twice-born one, is the secret enjoined by the scriptures:
namely, the worship of the liṅga of Śiva, practiced by Brahmā and the other gods, / which quells all sins and destroys all calamities.
It grants enjoyment and liberation; therefore, perform the worship of Śiva, / if the auspicious worship of the liṅga of Śiva does not slip away, O sage.
He who would interrupt the worship of Śambhu—by him my head would be cut off! / Better is being cast upon a trident, better is being dragged on a thorny silk-cotton tree,
better is the abandoning of life—never the omission of worship! / Better is falling into fire, better is being turned upside-down,
better is the eating of one's own excrement—not the omission of the worship of the Lord! / For the vile man who eats without having worshipped Īśāna—
his food is called the eating of sins in the form of food. / If one eats or chews without uttering the name of Śambhu,
[he commits sin]. The auspicious name 'Śiva'—in whose speech it proceeds, / tens of millions of his grave sins quickly turn to ashes.
The human who, having circumambulated Śiva, bows down, / attains that merit which comes from circumambulating the earth.
Having made three circumambulations and a five-fold prostration, / and circumambulating again and bowing, he is freed from sins.
Whoever plays all musical instruments or has them played in the abode of Śiva, / endowed with great strength, is born there to be served by the Vedas.
He who recites the Purāṇas to the three-eyed god of gods, / freed from all sins, the virtuous one dwells in the realm of Śiva.
To him the Lord always speaks pleasant words with affection. / Thus, in brief, has been declared the supreme worship of the Lord.
And you have a short lifespan, O twice-born one; practice the worship of Śiva, / either three times [a day], or twice, or even once,
or perform the worship of Śiva for a watch, or half a watch. / Having entered the forest-dweller stage of life, having made refuge as a forest-dweller,
worship Śaṅkara in the morning with wild flowers of the forest, / with bilva fruits, hundred-petalled lotuses, and fragrant water lilies,
with kadamba, hibiscus, punnāga, oleander, and trumpet flowers, / with tulasī, arka leaves, and likewise with aparājitā,
with apāmārga leaves, rudrajaṭā, and damanaka, / and with bilva leaves and thorn-apple blossoms, having equal fruits with all these,
with droṇa flowers, śirīṣa, śakta blossoms, dūrvā grass, and buds, / with nandyāvarta, unbroken rice grains, mixed with sesame or alone,
and with others according to one's capacity, one should worship Śiva in the morning. / The worship of Śiva may be done with karṇikāra blossoms, with golden ones, or even with dūrvā grass.
One should not worship the god with buds or with campaka flowers, except for water-born ones; / and among all water-born flowers, leaves, and unbroken rice grains,
kuśa grass flowers, and those made of silver or gold, / having prepared other things according to rule, whatever is cooked in oil, O king,
that is not declared stale; cakes and similar foods will do. / That which is sprinkled, accompanied by fruit, with oil, salt, acid, and cumin,
and roots, fruits, vegetables, and the like sprinkled in water, O king, / is not called stale, nor are the water of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
all water from great rivers, and water from Kedāra, / whatever holy site is in the form of a lake, or a holy site that is a well, O Rāghava,
and whatever water of tanks, step-wells, and pools is drawn by a well— / all that water of a holy site does not become stale.
Water should not be fetched at night; one should obtain water by day. / It should be kept containing sand, and it is not stale; this is beneficial.
Knowing this, you should perform worship upon the liṅga of Śiva. / Śambhu said: / Having been thus addressed by the sage, Ikṣvāku, dear to the brāhmaṇas,
intent on the worship of Śiva, remained for eight days. / Then, when the ninth day arrived, having performed worship in the morning,
when the moment of death arrived, having performed the worship of Śiva, / he surrendered his own vital breaths as an offering to the Great Lord.
Knowing him to be dead, the messengers of Yama arrived; / they stood making an effort to convey him to the realm of Yama.
The attendants of Śiva, headed by Vahnimukha, also arrived; / between them arose a dispute, saying, 'He is mine! He is mine!'
Then the messenger of Yama, noose in hand, afflicted the attendant of Śiva; / then Vahnimukha, enraged, thereupon [struck] the hundred messengers of Yama.
Having assumed a huge body and seized them with his hand, / crushing their heads with one hand, he cut them down like young grass.
Having killed the messengers, he took Ikṣvāku and departed; / and he presented him to the wise Vīrabhadra.
And he presented him to Śaṅkara, and the Great Lord said to him: / 'By you worship was performed for only eight days, day by day in the dark fortnight.
Formerly you reviled me, saying, 'The liṅga is indeed the tip of the penis.' / By that very commission of sin you will have a penis for a face.
a circular opening at the tip of the penis, devoid of tongue, nose, and the like; / yet because you formerly spoke my name, you will also be able to speak.'
Then, by the word of the Lord, he instantly became such. / Śambhu said: / Whoever should daily hear this excellent narrative of the Purāṇa,
freed from the bondage of sins, will become a devotee of Śiva. / And he goes to the abode of Śiva, and the speaker likewise [attains it].
And whoever tells this story becomes equal to Hara. / Having formerly recited this story, a king named Adhīra,
having committed sins, went to heaven together with his wife.

5.110.m: The glorious Rāma said: / This Fire, named Agniśikha, is indeed an attendant of Śiva; / how did he become like that? Tell me that, homage to you!
Śambhu said: / Formerly there was a certain kṣatriya, constantly prone to anger, / who had lost his wife, lost his army, lost his kingdom, and was exceedingly sorrowful.
Having obtained a pair of buffaloes, he took up farming together with his sons. / Laden with a huge debt, he was again exceedingly miserable.
Again the king was sorrowful due to the destruction of a son by a snake; / being in such a state, the ruler of the earth even abandoned agriculture.
Abandoning the two sons as well, having renounced food, he wept. / Then the two sons, approaching, spoke this to their father:
'For what purpose is this weeping, father? One who is lost does not return through weeping. / Your grief today will only serve to emaciate your body.
Through grief your two eyes are ruined, and your throat is ruined; / your religious practice is likewise ruined; why do you burn with grief?
One is lost and does not return; protect the five remaining lives! / The protection of many is meritorious, especially of dependents.
Why should you grieve for this enemy who has sought refuge with another?' / The father said: / 'How is a son an enemy, and how are you two sons enemies of mine?
Why did you speak of an extremely joyful son as an enemy?' / The two sons said: / 'While being born he carries away the wife; while growing up he carries away wealth;
while dying he likewise carries away vital breaths—what enmity could be greater than this? / And as for the pleasure that was mentioned by you, through touching, embracing, and the like—
all this ends in sorrow, O king, which I explain to you. / At the time of the son's birth, there is anxiety over the loss of the wife;
And while the wife is alive, there is the destruction of one's own happiness. / When impurity of the vagina has arisen, union is not possible.
When embracing tightly, their limbs are bathed in breast milk; / even if union takes place, the child's crying disturbs the woman.
Her mind is firmly fixed on the child, and from that arises distaste; / or if the infant falls down, sexual intercourse comes to an end in the middle.
When there is interruption in the middle of lovemaking, there is a sorrow like death. / In all that limited time, intercourse rarely happens;
at that time there is no food, and no sleep with the wife. / In protecting children there is distress through diseases, thirst, planetary afflictions, and the like.
That pleasure which is considered wonderful, such as climbing upon the father's lap, / or that caused by an embrace, dear one, or caused by kissing and the like,
the pleasures derived from exceedingly sweet speech and so forth, O ruler of men— / they do not equal a sixteenth part of the cessation in the middle of lovemaking.
And there are thousands of other sorrows in a son; / what can you achieve with this [son], who obstructs [good] in this world and the next?
Therefore abandon this grief; we two sons remain here.' / The king said: 'I shall abandon this grief, irresistible and obstructing all tasks.
My two sons, that which is beneficial for oneself in this world and the next must be done; / I shall go to my royal priest, my ancient great teacher,
to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, and he will give me my path.' / Having spoken thus, he went to the priest, the guru residing in Vārāṇasī.
He bowed down like a staff; then he was honored by the sage, / embraced, his head smelled, and a seat was offered to him.
And he was asked: 'Why have you come? What task may I do for you?' / The king said: 'Grant me the path, O priest, for crossing over saṃsāra.
I am constantly afflicted by worldly action; I have come to you for refuge.' / Vasiṣṭha said: 'See the goal, the great liṅga standing as Viśveśvara.
Worship this god of gods who holds the Pināka, O king of kings, / by worshipping whom formerly the sage Śakti, son of Arundhatī,
though devoured by a rakṣasa, did not go to the world of Yama; / he went to heaven for some time, and from there he went to the world of Brahmā.
From the world of Brahmā, my son remains sporting in the world of Viṣṇu. / Behold this hunter wandering in the forest, O great king,
worshipping Viśveśa with mere leaves collected by himself, / produced from the śamī tree, and with flowers of the areca palm.'
Behold him worshiping the Great Lord / with kadamba blossoms, arka flowers, and those grown from jasmine, and with these and others.
In merely half a watch from now, he will die; that is a marvel. / Indeed, when his time of death arrived, the hunter, in order to give a gift
to Śiva, saw a jar at his side / full of mango fruits, which was defiled by the leftovers of a dog and despised.
Because the planned offering was lacking, / the hunter uttered these auspicious words indicating devotion to people:
“In the absence of a flower, Hari offered an eye; in the absence of a fruit, the Sun offered a finger; / and in the slippage of the liṅga, the sage Jamadagni,
and when the base of the liṅga was split, split his body and offered it. / Other supreme acts of daring were done by other devotees of Maheśvara.
I too must act likewise; otherwise, I will share in fault.” / Meanwhile, a madman approached Śiva;
then, seizing the worship offered by the hunter, he instantly ate it, / and likewise vomited upon the pedestal of Śiva. Then the hunter
thought: “Shall I kill this wrongdoer to Śiva or not?” / Then, resolving solely upon his own death, Śaṅkara’s [devotee thought]:
“Just as the worship of Śiva offered by me was consumed by the madman, / this skin is indeed for covering the liṅga; therefore, for my soul,
this covering skin must quickly be shed by me today. / To relieve the worship, one should discard the obstruction of the loss of fruit.”
Having thus resolved, he wonderfully cut the skin with a sharp axe, / and having cut the skin of his right foot below the waist,
he quickly did the same to the left foot up to the waist. / Joyful yet trembling, he then cut upwards;
the hunter, having pierced the skin of his hands, belly, heart, and neck, / and having pierced the skin of his head, rejoiced.
Splitting the rounded flesh between them and taking it off with his fingers, / he cut it and offered the skin to the God.
Nearby, endowed with a divine form, with fair eyes, four-armed, / adorned with diverse ornaments, stood a Śaiva [attendant] in the sky.
Then Śaiva messengers arrived by hundreds and thousands, / bearing varied crowns and adorned with all ornaments,
all holding tridents in hand, resembling pure crystal, / four-armed, handsome, and standing on excellent celestial chariots,
all equal to the sun, calm, accompanied by beloveds like Rambhā, / endowed with sons, wives, power, zeal, and hundreds of amorous women.
Resembling the sun in brilliance, they showered a rain of flowers. / Summoned by them, the hunter did not go, and spoke to them:
“Should I go together with my wife and kinsfolk, or not?” / Hearing his word, the Śaivas then said these words:
“By whomsoever merit or sin is committed, its fruit must be experienced by him alone.” / The hunter said: “For all defilements and dharmas there is a single agent;
yet the fruit of the dharmas of Maheśvara extends even to two or many.” / In the meantime, Vīrabhadra arrived with a hundred attendants,
accompanied by many crores of gaṇas: “Come, hunter, with your relatives; / all has been said by you, and so it is, with your wife, kinsmen, and relations.
Ascending this celestial chariot, go to Śiva; may there be welfare for you all!” / Then, by his word, seated in the celestial chariot, he reached the world of Śiva.
Vasiṣṭha said: / “You have seen everything. Perform worship of the Lord; / freed from the bond of sin, you will go to the world of Śiva.
If kingship is desired by you, clean the courtyard of the Lord, O king, / and constantly apply the smearing of cow dung and water.
By this much, dominion over the earth will certainly be yours. / As long as your lifespan lasts, you will have kingship, and in the end the abode of Śiva.
The attainment of kingship cannot happen in this [life] after death; / therefore, having obtained another body by the power of serving Śiva,
kingship will belong to you, and your devotion to Śiva will be firm.” / Śambhu said: / Then, having performed worship in that manner, he died and went to heaven.
Attaining a royal birth again, devoted to Śiva, he ruled the kingdom. / Once the king went to the temple of the God,
filled with various lamps, like the King of Serpents with jewels. / Then, in the press of soldiers, one lamp fell on the king.
Then, enraged, taking the lamp swiftly, / the king, full of anger, hurled it into the lovely city of the temple.
The temple of the God was burnt by him, and sin accrued [to him]. / Then, the dwellings, houses, and other buildings that were burnt there,
the king had rebuilt, and then worshiped Maheśāna. / Then, when the day of death arrived, the king who had propitiated Śaṅkara,
bathing in ashes, lying in ashes, muttering the Rudra [hymn], died. / Having gone to the world of Śiva, he was addressed by Vīrabhadra:
“Become a tiger among the gaṇas, my own attendant; / by my command, bring Śiva's devotees into my presence.”

"And you will be headless, and you will become flame-mouthed."
He, however, spoke to the high-souled Vīrabhadra, the lord of gaṇas:

"The collection of [organs in] the head is the eyes, ears, likewise the tongue, nose, and mouth.
Without these, how will my activity be possible?

Or what sin was committed by me, O lord, in the absence of a head?"
Vīrabhadra said: "Formerly, an exceedingly beautiful courtesan was accepted by you.

Daily she [adorned] the temple of Maheśa with four-colored powders:
with the auspicious svastika, the sarvatobhadra, the nandyāvarta, and others;

with the lotus, the blue water-lily, the swing-bench, the fan, and the chowries;
the trident, the conch, the discus, the mace, and also the bow;

the trident, the drum, the sword, the bull, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Śiva;
likewise the eight-petaled lotus, and other mystical diagrams.

Drawing [these] every day, she worshiped the bull-bannered god.
Then once, that courtesan was present in the temple of the god.

A prison-guard of the king entered the temple of the god.
Then, seeing her there, he spoke these words:

The prison-guard said:
'A courtesan stationed in solitude! I am young and not old.
A woman should abandon an old man, a diseased man, a eunuch, an impotent man, a man devoid of wealth,

a wretched man with a short penis,
one who is beardless, covered with dirt, foolish, corrupted by foul odor.

A woman should avoid from afar even one who has minor vices.
Therefore, O courtesan, let sexual intercourse be given to me! Revive me quickly!'

The courtesan said:
'Devotion to one's husband is the supreme duty of women, which is fixed for all castes
and grants happiness here and in the hereafter—so indeed we have heard.

When a courtesan is dependent upon someone, she does not unite with another at that time;
she is renowned as a devoted wife; therefore, she must observe that.'

The prison-guard said:
'If that is so, death will come quickly, there is no doubt.'
Then, having gone near the king, he said this to the king:

'A courtesan is indeed a courtesan, not a wife; it is not fitting to say "no".'
Having spoken thus to the king, he then [took] gruel made from sour gruel.

Taking a little, he went to her house.
Seeing an opportunity while she slept, and stretching out his hand then,

the evil-minded one threw the gruel there into an opening in her garment.
Having done so, he then went and said this to the king:

'O king, having gone out and reached the foremost courtesan among your women,
after awakening that courtesan, you ought to inspect all her limbs,

or carefully examine the garment whose knot has been undone.'
Then the king, at the prison-guard's word, went to the house of the courtesan.

He said this: 'She is asleep; I am going to inspect her. Do you watch?'
He, however, said to the king there: 'O king, this is not proper for me.

Employ her mother or her father to inspect her;
upon their inspection, all this will quickly become clear.'

Then the mother was brought by the king, ready to look;
and at the word of the king himself, she was as if cleaning the garment.

Then, discovering the gruel present there, the mother rubbed it;
from the rubbing, the garment became wet. The king said, 'What is that?'

'It is nothing, your majesty, it is nothing,' said the mother of the courtesan.
Then the king, with much talk, seeing the garment with suspicion,

said, 'This garment is soaked with semen; let this be looked at!'
Then, having looked, those standing near said to the king, 'It is so.'

Then the king, having gone to his house, spoke to the magistrate:
'Right now, cut off the head of the courtesan without deliberation!

Her head must be shown to me within an hour.'
And the punisher, upon the king's word, having done so, showed [it] to him.

you will know taste; you will be intelligent, [though] exceedingly angry.'
Śambhu said:
Thus the king, devoted to Maheśvara, became flame-mouthed and unforgiving.

Therefore, one who desires happiness in the next world and in this one must be forgiving.
Whoever listens constantly to this unsurpassed, holy narrative,
freed from the bondage of sin, will abide in the world of Śiva."

5.111.m:
Śrī Rāma said:
"The glorification of Maheśa's name and the glorification of his worship,
the glorification of bowing down, and the glorification of gazing [upon him],

the glorification of giving water, of offering incense, O best of beings,
of offering lamps, perfumes, and so on—tell me, O teacher!"

Formerly, in the Tretā age, there was a king named Vidhṛta, full of valor.
When his father died, he, a boy, was consecrated in the kingdom on earth.

He made all those of the same age stay near him;
those who were old and those who were wise were not approved by him.

The young, wicked, doers of what ought not to be done were approved,
and those skilled in abducting good women, proficient in deeds of theft,

delighting in buffoonery, skilled in dancing, were approved by him,
those knowing mantras of subjugation, and those knowing about cloths and herbs,

and those accustomed to singing and dancing, rogues skilled in gambling, were dear [to him].
That king made an abandonment of those who had acted with his father's approval.

Having deliberated with them, he caused work to be done by the wicked;
he employed such and other wicked people.

Relying on their word, he abandoned educated friends;
those who would thump their chests with their fists and make howls were dear to him,

those who knew the essence of female genital marks, and were proficient in the lore of sexual enjoyment.
Then that kingdom became devoid of political wisdom.

Elephants, horses, chariots, camels, goats, cows, buffaloes, and the like, whatever there was—
all that came to ruin due to plunder here and there.

Then jewels and agricultural grains were not seen in the city.
Then he, defeated by another king, fled.

Then, having gone to a great forest, he made a mountain fortress;
and there, with a small retinue, he took recourse to the occupation of a thief.

Pointing out gold, clothes, grain, and the like, jewels, perfumes, and so forth,
here and there, thieves, deceivers of visitors,

he caused bindings and the like to be done by them in the work of seizing property.
When there was no food, he provided food at that time:

with the meat of cows, buffaloes, and so on; if grain was not obtained,
he arranged meals with horse-flesh and human flesh.

Such was his conduct, devoid of twilight worship and the like.
He had one minister, a rākṣasa named Surāpa,

who engaged him at all times, saying, 'Bring! Strike!'
Thus standing in the opinion of the rākṣasa, that abode of mercilessness,

with a retinue of a thousand men, would seize men who had gone to various lands.
Having found out about women who were pleasing to himself, he abducted them.

And having enjoyed them for a short time, he ate their meat.
Thus killing men and women, he ruled an unbearable realm.

Thus having ruled for a thousand years, that lowest of men,
with all his limbs slackened by old age, marred by wrinkles and grey hair,

the place for ten yojanas all around became lifeless.
Then the day of death arrived for that mighty king.
When the time of death arrived, the king, bathed and lying on the ground, / was surrounded by all his attendants who stood near him.
The wine-drinking minister said: “What is my duty? Command me.” / Then the king, afflicted, his life breath departing, being barely able,
his life breath depleted below the navel, spoke some words: / “Strike, strike, take away, O lord of the Daityas, at all times!”
Having spoken thus, he died; then the messengers of Yama arrived, / intent on beating [him], and made varied efforts to bind [him].
The binding nooses were crushed, and their weapon-staffs were shattered / at the mere touch of his body; and that became like a marvel.
Then Death came in person and bound him with a noose. / Seeing even the noose of Death broken, Death thought:
“The death of all mortals has been seen; never has such a thing been seen anywhere.” / While Death was absorbed in this thought, the valiant Jvālāvaktra,
bearing a trident, sent by Vīrabhadra, suddenly arrived. / Seeing Jvālāvaktra, Death quickly fled.
Then Vahnimukha, seeing Death fleeing, [called out]: / “Hey, hey, thief, thief, stay, stay! Where will you go?
A thief is freed from sin by mere impalement on a stake.” / Speaking thus, he fixed Death, impaled upon a trident.
Placing the trident on his shoulder, tying up the messengers with a rope, / and taking them fastened in foot-shackles, he approached the king.
Placing him on an excellent celestial chariot adorned with song and instrumental music, / he then went into the presence of the hero [Vīrabhadra] and reported everything to him.
Vīrabhadra too [reported] all that to Śaṅkara of boundless soul, / who was being served by various assemblies of sages, and by the gods led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
to the God accompanied by Pārvatī; / having bowed and reported, and [showing] Death upon the trident,

the valiant Vīrabhadra, the soul of all, became silent. / Seeing Agnyānana and reproaching him, Śiva [said]: “How was this bold act done by you, O gaṇa? / How do you not fear Death, who is greater than Yama? Tell me everything truthfully.”
Bowing to him, Vahnimukha, exceedingly angry, seeing Death, danced with joy / and said: “Theft was committed by Death; therefore he has been impaled by me on a trident.”
Śiva also released Mṛtyu, and made all the messengers free of pain. / Beholding Mṛtyu, Śiva spoke: ‘My name is present in these [beings] at the time of death.

Even if the name has missing letters or extra syllables, in the mind of another and with mind directed toward Me, / I truly give my very own world [to him], for he has spoken the name: "Strike!" (prahara)
They utter the word, giving the status of Hari merely by the prefix "pra-" added [to "hara"]. / Bow down from a distance to those reciting them, and convey my word to Yama.

Those who are devoted to bowing, asceticism, praise, and worship, to servitude and service, and speak according to the Veda, / who recite the five-syllable mantra and the Śatarudrīya hymn of Śiva—they are not to be questioned [by you].
Whoever wears my name, rudrākṣas, and sacred ash, and who recites the Purāṇa in my presence— / even if all sins exist in them, I govern them, not the authority of Yama.
Even those men deceitful and full of sins, who enjoy the food, clothing, and wives of others, / but who meet death in Vārāṇasī, or mortals at Śrīśaila—they are not to be questioned.
Lice, gnats, and bedbugs, animals and the like, insects and ants, / reptiles, scorpions, and pigs—those that die in Kāśī attain Śaṅkara.
Whoever, reciting this name, meditates in the lotus-temple of the heart / on Tryambaka, Virūpākṣa, Soma, adorned with the crescent moon,
the three-eyed one, whose eyes are the three Vedas, whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire— / having bowed to him, remain at a distance, O Mṛtyu, by my command.’
Then, having heard what Śiva said, Mṛtyu praised Śaṅkara: / ‘Salutations to you, O Lord of deities! Salutations to you whose form is divine!
Salutations to you, the omniscient one! Salutations to the Lord of beasts!’ / Then the god Mahādeva said to Mṛtyu: ‘Choose a boon.’
‘I am pleased by this hymn of praise.’ Mṛtyu requested a boon: / ‘Protect your own, O Lord, and protect me, a sinner, O Śaṅkara.’
Having said, ‘So be it,’ the Lord spoke to Mṛtyu: ‘Go, my child.’ / He went to the world of Yama and told everything to Yama.
Śambhu said: / ‘Whoever hears daily this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative / is freed from all sins and goes to the presence of Śaṅkara.’
